note: Short texts in our own words. Figures as given in the project brief; checking them against the source and the link check are still due before launch (PRD F-02.2a, F-02.3).

items.headline: This is as high as Earth goes.
items.body: The summit of Mount Everest stands about 8,849 m above sea level, higher than any other mountain. Yet another peak lies farther from the centre of the Earth.
items.compare: Stacked on top of each other, almost 27 Eiffel Towers would reach its summit.

pair.text: Its counterpart: the Challenger Deep, the lowest point of the oceans

items.headline: Everest would sink without a trace.
items.body: The deepest known point of the oceans lies in the Mariana Trench, about 10,935 m below the surface. Put Mount Everest in it and its summit would still be some 2 km under water.
items.compare: The water presses down here with more than 1,000 times the pressure at the surface.

pair.text: Its counterpart: Mount Everest, the highest mountain on Earth

items.headline: The Sahara only comes second.
items.body: No hot desert on Earth is larger; it stretches from the Atlantic to the Red Sea. The title of largest desert of all goes to a continent of ice.
items.compare: Almost as large as the United States.

pair.text: Its counterpart: Antarctica, the largest desert in the world

items.headline: The world’s largest desert is white.
items.body: What makes a desert is not heat but how little precipitation falls. Deep inside Antarctica hardly any snow arrives all year, which makes the frozen continent the largest desert on Earth.
items.compare: About 70 degrees colder than a household freezer.

pair.text: Its counterpart: the Sahara, the largest hot desert

items.headline: A lake almost five Eiffel Towers deep.
items.body: Lake Baikal is about 1,642 m deep, deeper than any other lake on Earth. By volume it is also the largest freshwater lake.
items.compare: It holds about a fifth of all the fresh water in the world’s lakes and rivers.

items.headline: A white patch you can see from space.
items.body: The largest salt flat on Earth lies in the high Andes. The bright, almost perfectly level surface stands out at once on satellite images.
items.compare: About four times the size of Luxembourg, yet its height varies by less than a metre.

items.category: Tallest mountain from base to peak
items.headline: Taller than Everest, mostly under water.
items.body: Mauna Kea rises 4,207 m above the sea, but its foot lies deep on the floor of the Pacific. Measured from there, the volcano is more than 10,000 m tall.
items.compare: From its foot on the sea floor, it is more than a kilometre taller than Mount Everest.

pair.text: Compare: Mount Everest, the highest above sea level

items.headline: The closest you can get to the stars.
items.body: The Earth bulges at the equator. That is why the summit of Chimborazo, only 6,263 m above sea level, lies farther from the centre of the Earth than any other point on its surface.
items.compare: Its summit lies about 2 km farther out into space than the top of Mount Everest.

pair.text: Compare: Mount Everest, the highest above sea level

items.headline: Water falls for almost a kilometre.
items.body: Angel Falls drops from the edge of the table mountain Auyán-tepui, 979 m in all, higher than any other waterfall on Earth. Much of the water turns to mist before it reaches the bottom.
items.compare: About as high as three Eiffel Towers stacked on top of each other.

items.headline: A tower that sees the sun set twice.
items.body: The Burj Khalifa rises 828 m above Dubai and has been the tallest building in the world since 2010. From its top floors the sun sets a few minutes later than in the street below.
items.compare: More than twice as tall as the Empire State Building in New York.
items.source: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat

items.headline: The hottest air ever measured.
items.body: On 10 July 1913, a thermometer at Furnace Creek showed 56.7 °C, still the highest air temperature on record. Nearby Badwater Basin lies 86 m below sea level, the lowest point in North America.
items.compare: Almost as hot as a cup of tea you can just about drink.
items.source: WMO Weather and Climate Extremes Archive

items.headline: Places where rain is a rumour.
items.body: Some weather stations in the Atacama have never recorded a drop of rain. The dry, clear air is why some of the world’s largest telescopes stand here.
items.compare: Germany gets about a thousand times as much rain in a year.

items.headline: Built by animals, seen from space.
items.body: Around 2,900 reefs and 900 islands stretch along the coast of Queensland, built by billions of tiny coral animals. It is the largest structure made by living things.
items.compare: About as long as the way from Berlin to Lisbon.
items.source: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority

items.headline: A jungle grows inside this cave.
items.body: Where parts of its ceiling collapsed, sunlight falls into Hang Sơn Đoòng and a forest grows underground. Its main passage is more than 5 km long.
items.compare: A 40-storey skyscraper would fit inside its largest chamber.

items.headline: The neighbours live 2,400 km away.
items.body: About 250 people live on this volcanic island in the middle of the South Atlantic. There is no airport; the only way there is a ship journey of about a week from Cape Town.
items.compare: Cape Town, the nearest city, is about 2,800 km away, farther than London is from Moscow.

items.headline: Your nearest neighbours may be astronauts.
items.body: Point Nemo is the spot in the oceans farthest from any land. When the International Space Station passes overhead, its crew is closer than the nearest people on the ground.
items.compare: The ISS orbits about 400 km up; the nearest island is almost seven times farther away.
